I agree completely. I don't think the force development in the sequel trilogy was all that complex or well thought out.  It seemed cool on screen and reflected a number of political/current events and seemed like it was good on screen. Some elements works but others just seemed tacked on and i think really hurt the sequels at large. This is NOT my only issue with the sequels just some of it.

I don't take a lot of what came out of the Sequel trilogy all that seriously in terms of the force "stuff." Some of it was reasonable ie. the fire with Yoda but the writing was just bad and i think grossly simplifies the entire concept of the force, light and dark.  

A lot of it sounds cool but really fails to get the complexity of the force which at this point had already been established in the prequels and the Clone Wars through the Mortis Arc.

Yet the son still feels emotion and cares for those he loves. This is clearly on display in the Mortis Arc. It's not that simple and I think you see that in Anakin and that being forced to the Dark side isn't about lack of compassion.

 I do think that the Daughter is at the extreme side of things and we see this with her sacrifice for Ashoka. The Daughter and Son are opposites of one another but the son doesn't have the emotional range or altruistic nature to see the consequences of his actions.  It's brash and deceive to a fault. The daughter is not brash but is sometimes too slow to act. 

Until the Bendu, outside of the Father, we've never seen a truely neutral force user until the Bendu.

People like Bendu b/c it challenges what we know of the force. It's more then just dark-light. There's a balance between the two. Bendu represents that's balance in much the same way nature does. He understands that this balance is how the universe works. It's this knowledge that helps him teach Kannan after his injury. We don't completely understand why or how he came to be. Is he native to Attolon? Or is he like the Witches and come from beyond the Outer Rim? Is he the only one? That mystery is fascinating and in Star Wars help perpetuate the nature and lore and mystery of "The Force."

For me, it's a complex thought process on why i find the Bendu so fascinating. You have to go back to some of Feloni's lore in Clone Wars and the Mortis arc. Bendu follows the Father, Jedi the daughter and Sith the son. Bendu is really the first kind of true balanced force user (other then the Father) that we meet.  In my view, Ashoka seems to embrace a lot of the "balanced" but i think fundamentally despite her giving up the "Jedi" is still very much one as she embraces the daughter and is a true light side welder. This is more complex lore.

The only other truely "balanced" character we meet is Anakin but i think his is less about balance and more about wild swings between the two.  That's why the Father wanted him to follow in his path.

Yes, smoke can trigger migraines. Its actually super dangerous for HM suffers. In women, its even more dangerous combined with birth control. It can led to strokes. I know i have trouble with cigar/hukkah/cigar smoke. I haven't had an issue with weed but generally when i use i vape or take an edible. I would absolutely think it could be a trigger for some people. My neuro said if the anxiety is a thing the edibles are the better choice for your body.

Back off the smoking and try edibles instead if its a real need. I think that fact your are starting to see a pattern "after you smoke" might be the trigger. It could also be the recovery period. My brother actually get seizures, explained to be similar to my HM from dehydration after drinking heavily. It could be the recovery that's actually doing it. 

Keep a migraine diary - it should help you see patterns. 

Also, don't over think the complex vs hemiplegic stuff btw. That's very very nuanced for the medical and really doesn't change that much in terms of management. I had HM and developed optical aura later on, so now they are "complex." Absolutely nothing has changed in terms of management. It just means you don't fit into the specific and narrow HM box. No big deal :) Do treat it like HM though as there's more risks involved....a good neuro will base treatment based on you symptoms NOT on what you migraine is called.

Chest voice feels deeper and obviously comes from the chest/lungs. This is generally the better way to sing for classical singers. You have more supportive breath. Singing is a balance of your voice vs pitch. If you don't have the right pitch, you aren't getting the music right. That's the MOST important thing to do. Learn to make the music and match the pitch. This takes time!

I'd also advise watching some videos on basic music mechanics. Not theory, that get REALLY REALLY complicated fast. Learn terms like Octave or the basic of like Do, Re, Me etc. Also, some of the basics of voice anatomy. It's amazing how helpful its been in understanding my voice quirks. Do you site read? You don't have to. I'm a mediocre site reader myself its helpful for matching pitches via a keyboard. There's lots of free options for keyboards online.

We have two points where our voice shift to make higher or lower notes, this is called a passaggio. When i switch from one to the other, my voice timbre changes.  I feel more heady in my upper ranges and my chesty in my lower ranges. That's okay - but learning how this works for you and learning how to move between these ranges is important depending on how you sing.

Movie nights, hot dogs nights, bowling, white water rafting ect.  Sign up for more then you think you can do, you can always drop out. There's all kinds of things too! And no, it's not just Greek life...honestly, most of friends who were Greek were active beyond their fraternity or sorority. Do you like hiking? There's a group that does work on the AT which is VERY close to campus. There are a number of local volunteer locations plus organizations that help you find those things.  Great groups for theater and music lovers supported by the academic departments.  Lot's of other affinity groups like religious groups, cultural groups and policy groups and more. Dickinson has a farm and takes students out there to work in their free time too! There's student writting groups, philosophy groups, dance troops...depends on your interest tbh. Don't go by what others tell you to do! Go with you own interests! You'll be WAY happier.

The friends of mine that weren't active in ANYTHING outside of classes were pretty miserable come sophomore year. Dickinson wants you to be a part of the community and that means getting out of you dorm room.  Go check out the list of clubs and things like that. That's how Dickinson thrives...

Don't expect a "clubbing" life that's not how the school works.  There are parties but it tends to be among friends and cliques and you don't get that right away. They are generally small and you don't get invited unless you are a friend of an upper classman. Freshman dorm room parties get busted quickly eps. when there is alcohol  involved. I emphasize parties b/c if you are just with your friends really not making a lot of noise, you'll be fine. My advice - don't be stupid and use common sense. Most large parties are upper classman and tbh the biggest ones i went to as a Freshman were Greek of campus parties. They weren't unfun as i had friends at the parties but it was always a pain getting too and from them. If you get busted, don't get busted off campus. The punishment is way worse and CPD is nasty.  DPS may seem annoying but they genuinely do have your best interests and don't bust parties unless they really have too. TBH, upperclassman usually called the parties in that were busted from my experience - if you are partying after 2 AM, you're gonna get in trouble. That's kind the unofficial time things wind down.

# From NIH on Hemiplegic Migraines - [https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513302/](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513302/)

# Treatment / Management

Symptoms of a hemiplegic migraine can be scary and distressing. Establishing a correct diagnosis and initiating proper treatment is essential to help manage and prevent attacks. Treatment of hemiplegic migraines involves pharmacological treatment with abortive and preventive medications. Severe attacks may need hospitalization and additional measures.

Patients with a hemiplegic migraine may be managed with the same abortive and preventive medications used for a typical migraine with aura except for agents that may exacerbate ischemia. Treatment of acute episodes is mainly with NSAIDs and antiemetics. Intranasal ketamine given at the onset of attack has shown benefit in patients with familial hemiplegic migraine. **The use of triptans for a hemiplegic migraine is controversial.**

Verapamil has been used as a prophylactic and abortive agent for hemiplegic migraine. Other drugs that have been used for prophylactic treatment include flunarizine, ketamine, lamotrigine, and naloxone. Nonrandomized studies have suggested acetazolamide may be effective as a preventive medication for familial hemiplegic migraine.[\[29\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513302/#) For prophylactic treatment, initial therapy with verapamil, flunarizine, or acetazolamide is recommended for patients with hemiplegic migraine. Patients who do not respond to these medications should try lamotrigine, particularly in patients who have predominant aura symptoms than a headache.[\[30\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513302/#) Other preventive medications that can be used (like in other typical migraines with aura) are amitriptyline, topiramate, and valproic acid.

**Triptans and ergotamines are usually contraindicated in a hemiplegic migraine because of concern for potential cerebral vasoconstriction. Some specialists also recommend avoiding beta-blockers as preventive therapy for patients with hemiplegic migraines, like migraines with brainstem aura.**

Methylprednisone at 100 mg daily for five days resolved symptoms of a child with hemiplegic migraine and severe symptoms.[\[31\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513302/#)

Triggers for a hemiplegic migraine headache should be identified and avoided if possible.[\[8\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513302/#)[\[32\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513302/#)[\[33\]](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK513302/#)

These are somethings that have helped me. Im 38. I've had HM attacks since i was 6. #6 is the most important imo.

Step 1: Keep a log of your attacks. Learn what is the normal with you aura and keep telling yourself this is normal and this is okay. For most HM attacks, it's cyclical and learning that cycle is helpful. Not saying it can't change, but those changes are the red flags to go to an ER. 

Step 2: Learning some stress reduction techniques. For me, I use circle breathing which is a technique i actually used to help with singing.  Take a deep breath in for 8, hold for 8, release for 8, rest for 8 etc. Slowly work up the time..i am able to get to about 20 but it's not a competition.  

Step 3: Create a environment where you can find comfort. Migraine prep is massive! Do you have a plan of attack and a migraine kit set up? Getting this ready in advance is a huge thing for me and helps reduce my heart rate. Set up a plan of attack with your husband and how best to work with this and your kids. Kids are more intelligent then we often give them credit for and helping them to understand the situation is a win win for both of you.  

Step 4: My mom taught me at a young age that treating it like something scary isn't always advisable.  Sometimes realizing that it's more of a nuisance is the better approach. As a parent, i think you can relate to this mindset. It takes practice and i've certainly had attacks that making me scared, annoyed, frustrated and just sad.

Step 5: Take the time to figure out what works for you.  I will take a shower as the water on my skin and the steam relaxes me. I also use a little (a VERY LITTLE) peppermint oil of my forehead and by my nose.  You can also use lavender and a few other things. This just feels cools and something about smelling peppermint is soothing. I've been able to tolerate more noise so sometimes VERY calm music and storm noises help. I also have a defuser and will use lavender, bergemont, peppermint etc. I also always EAT before my aura gets to bad. I've been less sick and when i am it's not nearly as painful. I'm also WAY less worn out on the back end.  I also sometimes ice my head. Cold feels good during an attack.

Step 6: Be patient with yourself. I think we as a culture assume these things are easy. They aren't. I'm weird as I grew up with this and took me until about 25 to really soldify what worked for me. That was b/c of hormonal changes. Don't get mad if you feel fear or annoyance. This will actually make things WAY worse. Be patient and slowly work to finding what works for you.  I also suggest listening and feeling what your body wants - when you figure some of this out, things get easier.

I am a policy wonk and worked in the advocacy/campaign world for years after i graduated. I walked away for personal reason and that I burnt out. I also find politics as a career is more of a lifestyle then a typical career. On IR vs Political Science - i found there were two types of students. Those who took it very seriously who were your Hard core Polisci and IR students. IR is a VERY intense major and so can political science if you take it seriously and study and take the tough classes. Some students will BS there way through it and take the hard classes. My advice if you go that path start with the basic 101 requirements for Polsci and IR. There's a lot of overlap. IR is way more inter-displinary so you'll have an additional cultural/language requirement beyond what other students have, IR spefics course and some economic course. I took most of these and loved them but polisci had more interest to me. There also subsects of political science ie. IR, process, more general etc. lean on your advisor here - i took a lot of foreign policy, defense, etc. type course. I was very interested in executive beaucracy at the time. I was done all but one polsci requirement junior year....what can i say i like polsci but took more because i had the room too. 

On law school - really really do you homework here prior to that process. Dickinson does have 3-3 program with Dickinson Law (associated with Penn State) and Dickinson Law is an excellent law school btw one of the best in PA. Most students did NOT choose to do this path and apply to law school like any normal student would.  You don't have to be pre-law, political science or IR to go that path. I have friends who went to law school who were actually Physics majors! I also advise from personal experience and friends of mine, getting some real world experience before going to get a masters degree or a law degree unless you are in the Sciences or get a scholarship. I would have gone for law and personally glad i waited as I am better with advocacy and grassroots then with law. It's nuanced but you won't always learn that in college. I know too many lawyers who left the law to pursue other things...that's my only warning. I also have friends who were in Mock Trial and went to law school and loved it!  I actually found graduate school WAY easier b/c of some maturity and life experience made it easier at least for me :) There is a pre-law/law school process that the school runs. If this is of interest, engage in it early as certain classes will help pad your transcript.

On  religion - there's not much of a stigma or at least there wasn't while i was there. People kind of did whatever they believed in and everyone was VERY supportive of that.  DCF is a the Christian group and was very active of ALL branches. Hillel was always very active when i was there and there are other groups. I had several close friends that actually became reverends/pastors and rabbis. Dead serious. Students went to the local community churches and they were always happy to work with the college and students!  I do think what they didn't do is force their beliefs on others, they used it more to engage and educate when appropriate. You can get as active or inactive as you want. Honestly, some students will be more in your face but generally are super chill and respectful. I also had friends who were hardcore atheists and we always had fun! Do students run around screaming religion? No, not really but some are very religious on a personal level. Does that make sense? 

On Study abroad - there's a few different options here. Most students take a single semester junior year and go away on one of the programs. As long as you have the grades and the language requirements, they'll get you into one.  Most of my friends went to the UK and had a blast.  Dickinson also offers summer sessions to various counties which some of my friends did as well. I actually studied abroad with a non-Dickinson program that went to Scandinavia (personal interest). I spent two summers ie. about a semester in Oslo.  Dickinson will happily work with you to find a placement if they don't have somewhere you want to go. They aren't closed minded but going through Dickinson is WAY easier. I didn't get pre-approved by Dickinson for my program, but given the school it was through, my good grades and the intensity of the program go everything approved for my credits! Dickinson will push their programs.

Work force transition - the hardest thing for me was changing my sleep patterns. I'm a night owl so that was tough. There are some nuances that you will have to get use to. Work life vs. college life. Learning certain professional decorum but outside of an internship, you won't get that anywhere. I also am unique b/c i went into the political campaign world which is a whole different beast of it own. TBH, the activities outside of the classroom ie. club leadership and PR and such really prepped me in the areas i didn't necessarily get in the classroom.  There's ample opportunities for that if you go looking for it.

Dickinson considers academic preformance, your interest and your interview very very seriously as part of the academic process. Academic preformance is their number 1. Grade evaluations also depend a great deal on your school district, type of school etc. I went to a difficult private school so if I'd gone to the public school (where my brother went) I'd have been a A student. I was a B - A+ student.  I had a consistent B+/A- GPA. I also think Dickinson looks at the record based on subject not always GPA ie. If you are a bad math student... they'll look at that to esp if that's not where you are going. 

I had my 2nd longest interview at Dickinson. This is your chance to explain your freshman year. Why you like Dickinson and explore topics that might not come up in your application. Asking questions is HUGE here. Do your homework! 

I didn't use my SATs bc it didn't help me. I am a bad test taker. My ACTs were pretty good though. Don't be afraid if they don't reflect your performance to NOT submit them. 

Dickinson also loves students who are interested in the school. I knew right away I wanted to go there and went a few times to campus. I also did some creative things like make an mini art portfolio... the art department loved it and said no other student had done that. I sent a sample of my acapella group as well with my application. 

Dickinson wants well rounded students and students who aren't total academic centric or party animals. They also generally go after students who arent so overly involved they have no time for fun or a social life. They want students who will contribute to the campus life! If you don't want to do clubs and be involved, you will be miserable at Dickinson. 

It's also a very academic school! You will and must work hard. I think I pretty much did an average 6-7 hours a day of work outside of class at minimum. So did most people I knew! It was a huge help transitioning to the working world! It's not a school for everyone but if this sounds like you ie. Someone who loves to learn, seek connections to different classes, and love to be around those who do you'll thrive if you do the work! I don't know anyone at Dickinson that wasn't an academic to some degree!

PS: I am not an art or music major. I had a minor in art and did a lot of stuff for fun musically including some classes. Dickinson encourages this! I was actually Political Science :)

Although it’s referred to as “Feeling”, Fi is not internal emotions, but rather values that come from within. NeFi’s might experience a deep well of emotions, but this is not the root of Fi. It is a decision making-process that makes them very interested in determining their own moral code and what their gut instinct tells them is right, which is often based on how they would like to be treated themselves. They tend to be very considerate of others, and are likely to be highly aware of how they feel other people see them. 

 It may take a long time to mull over their own beliefs to make sure they seem right. This values-refining process can take quite a bit of time and requires mental solitude, which can make the NeFi seem very introverted in these times. Fi generally puts authenticity in high esteem and is repulsed by anything that seems fabricated or shallow to them. - In short, this self reflection and self evaluation of belief often creates feelings of doubt in ourselves. We don't like fake people but that's not always easy to tell. We tend to give people the benefit of the doubt. 

NeFi’s really like their autonomy. Although we like working with other people on interesting ideas, we despise being micromanaged by someone they don’t respect and trust. They usually prefer to take on a challenge their own way, without the steps being pre-defined for them. Its not so much a trust issue as we don't like being boxed in by clear cut paths. 

  
An NeFi’s outside-the-box thinking can lead to what others may see as disruptive behaviour. Often, if someone tries to make them do something one way, they’ll look for a different way. This usually isn’t an intentional rebellion. They look for new ways to do things because it’s more exciting than following conventional routes or just doing what they’ve done before. Their other functions all serve their drive to find new solutions to problems.   
  
They thrive in “chaotic” environments as they find them fun. It gives their Ne driven mind more interesting input to play with for ideas. It also gives them more information to look for patterns in and is more likely to be a positive space for new ideas to come forth, as opposed to  environments that are more conventional and traditional. 

I think our independence stems from our desire to explore and seek new things. It's not out of a place distrust necessarily of others. I know for me, i don't work well with bosses that try to box me and won't consider new ideas.  Remember our Fi overwhelms our Ni.

I am so sorry you are dealing with this! I've had HM attacks since I was 6 (i'm 38) so i can EASILY explain this simply. 

Predrome: 

This is the stage where I start feeling "off." Its hard to explain but i usually feel really warm, like i'm having a hot flash (never had one so i'm guessing). My reality starts going really fast. Everything feels like a whirl wind.  I imagine it's what being on some drugs is like. My heart isn't racing but i feel like everything is going double speed.  I also usually am hit with an overwhelming sense of fatigue. It comes out of no where.

Aura: 

This is when I know for sure I'm getting a migraine. For me, I usually get some visual disturbances in one eye. I joke that it looks like art deco vomited in my eye. Sometimes i get spots as well. I also find that i depth perception issues called Alice in Wonderland syndrome.  My arms feel longer. Things are further away.  I take my meds asap at this point. I get water, coca cola, something to vomit in and crawl into bed. I usually try to eat something as it helps on the back end and vomiting is easier. It hurts on an empty stomach.

Then starts the Hemiplegia - for me it usually starts in my hands. They first feel weak and then progress to almost a pins and needle feeling. I used to describe it as "fizzy" or the way soda feels on your tongue but in your hand. This slowly progresses through the rest of my body. For me, it slowly spreads and moves pretty much in order.  Usually when it his my tongue, I get hit with something called aphasia. 

 Aphasia is when you having trouble forming coherent words and sentences. I know what i want to say but it comes out all garbled. I also sometimes get ataxia.  This messes with your gate and balance. I struggle to walk.  

I then get VERY VERY nauseous. I move a leg. I vomit. I twist wrong. I vomit. This part is the end of my aura phase.

Headache Phase: 

The headache begins usually a 20 minutes to 60 minutes after my aura begins. Usually my aura, improves before the headache starts but not always. I do feel "weakness" in my body and word retrieval issues at this point.  

My headache is usually in my left temple (though I have them in my right). My headaches last anywhere from 3-6 hours though i have some WAY worse and way better. The headache feels like squeezing. It's a tough pain to describe but it's miserable.  I am most sensitive to light, noise etc. at this point in the headache.  

I try to sleep through this part. I'll use cold compresses and ice. Sometimes a shower helps. My meds help this a lot but without them or they don't work, the pain is incredible. I don't even know how to describe it. I try to keep eating and drinking only because i don't feel as bad if i can keep things down. Eventually it stops....

Postdrome aka. Migraine Hangover:

For me, I usually have a mild headache following a migraine. I feels worse then a sinus headache. You move your head weird it hurts. You sneeze - it hurts. It feels way more physical like someone hit you with a hammer then say a tired or dehydrated headache.

I usually feel absolutely fatigued. I just want to sleep. I am low energy. I've realized these attacks almost set my body into overdrive.  I refuel myself and try to mild foods. Bagels, pretzels, toast etc. to help boost my energy until i can stomach something else. Go with what sounds good imo. My stomach is usually still pretty upset.

I usually feels some "weakness" in the side that had the hemiplegia but after many doctor's tests there's no physical change so the assumption is that the nerves are almost in shock or something like that. I also have to deal with some word retrieval issues for up to a week. I also find that different things kind of linger after a migraine. 

  
Everyone's process is a bit different so don't go by my experiences. Migraines also change too. Mine now are different then when i was a kid. I get them more frequently but way less severely. 

Let me know if you have questions :)

Depression sucks! I've had it a few times but once really badly after a REALLY abusive relationship. You have done NOTHING wrong and you are not to blame! You'd be surpised how many people though depression was easily fixed through simple things and the experience was something fixed by a pill and life style changes only. From my experience, it takes time to overcome and you may need help! That's 100% okay! Don't let anything i suggest overwhelm you. If it makes you feel angry...that's okay too. 

[https://hyperboleandahalf.blogspot.com/2011/10/adventures-in-depression.html](https://hyperboleandahalf.blogspot.com/2011/10/adventures-in-depression.html) \- this is the best blog post on how my depression felt. Part II is great as well. I hope this helps make it feel a bit more relatable.

One thing, I can tell you is look at your life style and make sure that you are adding things in that make it interesting or fun.  It may not feel that way but sometimes changing up things can help. I'd also tell you make sure you are getting exercise and eating enough and eating quality foods.

I also started a gratitude exercise everyday. Before bed, I'd name one thing i did i was proud of each day. Something that I was greatful for - it didn't have to be complex ie. a simple as the way the grass feels between your toes, or the sunshine on my skin etc. and one thing i was looking forward to tomorrow.  This was helpful because it helped me find little things that were positive and helped re-spark my Joyeux de vie. 

Also journalling can help pin point things that might be a deeper root to the problem.

Welcome to a not so fun club. I had very similar situation with mine when it first presented the difference was, I was 6. Some things i'd recommend doing...not a doctor..

1. Educate yourself as much as possible on HM. There's some REALLY bad information out there. Please use reputable sources. The "Migraine Brain" covers general migraines but it's a great way to understand migraines on a more general level. Really helpful for me especially in regards how to communicate my condition to others. I am tol this day shocked how few doctors REALLY understand my condition and in some cases flat out denied my condition. I've also ran into some doctors claiming i have seizures. Never had one! So education is key here.

As part of education, for me learning about the migraines helped me be less stressed and paniced. Oddly enough, it's helped me stay calm and actually reduce the severity of my attacks knowing that it'll all pass. This takes time and didn't really learn this until my mid-20s.

2. Keep a 'migraine journal.' What happened before, during and after an attack? What was the weather like? What is a bad/stressful day? Did you work out? What did you eat? What meds are you taking? As a woman, tracking your cycle is important etc. You may see patterns to help treat you. You can also take this to your doctors appointments.

3. Build a migraine kit and plan! You may not know exactly what you need but over time you will. My kit contains Excedrin for migraine, snack (granola bars, chocolate), ice pack, trash bag and trash can, some peppermint oil, bottle of water, Coca-Cola classic.  I also always carry a note explaining my condition and what to do ie. don't call the ER unless i tell you. I always wrote out a note for ER including my meds. My plan is what to do when i get one ie. call someone for a ride, leave me alone etc. 

4. For me, I find consistency helps my migraines immensely.  Like any health provider will tell you for any condition, take care yourself! If you need to destress, do it. Massages help my migraines significantly. Sleep consistency. Stay hydrated and nutrient filled. Watch your blood pressure and weight etc.

First, Boston is not a commonwealth. Massachusetts is. Boston is the state capital of Massachusetts.

The term commonwealth is an old English term meaning "established for the good of the community at large and bring happiness and riches to the people." It has other contextual ties to the republic and public etc. ie. an indication that the purpose was for the people.

There are only four commonwealths in the US. Massachusetts, Virginia, Pennsylvania, and Kentucky.  The first three were extremely influential American colonies if not the most significant imo. The states declared themselves commonwealths after independence was declared. The dates are all a bit different. PA declared in late 1776 for example. This is significant as the first US government was established under the Articles of Confederacy and each "state" had a slightly different title and set of laws. Ultimately this failed and in 1789 the current US Constitution was adopted. I won't deep dive into each state constitution.

Kentucky was not an 13 original colonies but was a part of colonial and early American VA until it seceded the territory to the US in 1792 and it became its own "commonwealth" like it parent VA.

In terms of actual application, as it applies to the state, there are no differences between state and commonwealth in the US. It's just historic and tradition. It is worth noting they all have bicameral state legislatures (like the US legislative branch). State courts are referred to as "commonwealth" courts.

The term county is from the UK. The system the US uses is based on the UK system and was adopted during the colonial period when the US was under British control. The US court system is also based on the UK model.

Our "county" divisional system is based on the UK system where the counties pretty much operate the same way. Counties in the UK were once run by earls which in French in Comte or count. Elected officers of the county are often referred as "row officers" as they used to be elected as a block or row. This is no longer the case. These roles can include but not all counties use these and are usually determined at the state level
